places.how: Press Win + R, paste the path, press Enter.

places.what: Older zip installs from launch week and the alpha
places.path: Next to the extracted Luduvo folder, for example Downloads\windows-x86_64\Luduvo\
places.how: Open the folder you unzipped Luduvo into.
Press Win + R, paste the path, press Enter. It opens in Notepad.

places.what: Can't find the install? Use the Start menu
places.how: Press the Windows key, type Luduvo, right-click the first result and pick Open file location. If that opens a shortcut, right-click it and pick Open file location again.

places.what: The easiest way: run Luduvo from a terminal and copy what it prints
places.how: Open a terminal, run the command, and when it fails, copy everything it printed. You can paste it straight into the Doctor.

sources.label: Terminal output from a Fedora player

places.what: Log files, probably somewhere under here
places.how: Nobody has confirmed where Linux writes client.log, and some players say it doesn't write one at all.
LuduvoGame and LuduvoEditor live here. Running them from Terminal shows their output.
One error message showed /Library/Application Support/Luduvo. It may really be in your home folder's Library.
One Mac player could only find studio.log. crash.log was only announced for Windows.

facts.text: client.log is replaced every time Luduvo starts. Grab it straight after the game fails, before you try again.
crash.log only arrived in build 44, on Windows. It's often empty, which just means nothing crashed that time.
For client problems, client.log and crash.log matter most. For Studio problems, studio.log and crash.log.
Deleting client.log is harmless. Luduvo writes a new one next time.
